strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem setting: enabling users to provide human reasoning (with optional visual evidence patches) during VLM editing, which prior VLM editors (GRACE, BalancEdit, MSCKE, LiveEdit) do not support; this is a genuinely new editing setup with practical relevance.

Introduction of two new evaluation axes (rationale generality and chain-of-error generality) that go beyond standard reliability/locality/rephrasing metrics and probe a form of generalization not measured before.

The topology-aware embedding analysis (Newman modularity over image-text similarity networks, unimodal bias metrics, scale-invariance proofs in Appendix A) is a thoughtful and somewhat original contribution, with useful insights into vision/language bias across VLM layers (Fig. 6-7, 13) that could be of independent interest.

Extensive evaluation: 4 VLMs across 2 datasets, sequential editing experiments, thorough ablations (embedding choice, K, rejection threshold, key merging), and fair reasoning-enabled (COT) variants of all baselines so that baselines receive the same inputs.

ReasonEdit achieves strong results (e.g., R-Gen/CoE-Gen far above baselines) while preserving locality (1.00) and remaining competitive in per-edit time, and the paper includes an honest note on why some SOTA editors (MSCKE, LiveEdit) could not be included.
weaknesses: Potential circularity in the evaluation of the headline claims: R-Gen test questions are generated by GPT-4o from subsets of the same reasoning sentences that ReasonEdit stores verbatim in its codebook, and CoE-Gen scenarios are built to contain those same facts. Retrieval over stored facts may therefore trivially succeed because the test inputs paraphrase the stored values, inflating the paper's central 'new forms of generalization' results. The paper does not rule out this leakage (e.g., by comparing against retrieval over an irrelevant fact bank).

The method is essentially retrieval-augmented prompting: no model weights change and retrieved sentences are prepended to the prompt. The paper should more carefully defend this as 'editing' and, more importantly, ablate against a simple generic-retrieval baseline (e.g., SBERT text embedding alone, or a generic CLIP-style image-text retriever) to isolate how much gain comes from the topology-balanced dual embedding versus simply having any fact retrieval. The ablation compares VLM vision/language layers but not the obvious pretrained-text-encoder-only baseline.

The connection between modularity and downstream editing performance is validated only post hoc and qualitatively; there is no direct evidence that modularity rankings predict editing outcomes across settings, so 'principled' selection is somewhat overstated.

GRACE and GRACE-COT report essentially identical numbers in Table 1 (e.g., LLaVA FVQA: 0.98/0.69/0.92/0.54/0.76/0.99 for both), which is suspicious given that GRACE-COT stores additional reasoning entries that should change retrievals; this needs explanation or correction.

Evaluation is confined to multiple-choice VQA with answer selection via softmax over four options (Appendix D.1); this simplifies the real reasoning-heavy setting motivating the work, and the synthesized R-Gen/CoE-Gen evaluation data (GPT-4o questions, diffusion-generated images) introduces label noise of unquantified magnitude.

Key-merging yields only ~20% memory reduction with no accuracy change reported in the main table, so its practical value is marginal; and some hyperparameters (K=5, p=50) are set using the same datasets being evaluated.

Writing has recurring grammatical/editorial issues (e.g., 'none which we feel', 'each keys', 'prepend prepends', unclosed quotation in Sec. C), and the impact statement is boilerplate; minor but noticeable polish problems.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuinely underexplored problem setting: allowing users to supply reasoning chains (with visual evidence patches) when correcting VLM errors, and the motivation from realistic deployment scenarios is plausible.
The proposed evaluation axes (rationale generality, chain-of-error generality) are new and more informative than standard edit metrics for reasoning-heavy VQA.

Broad empirical coverage: four architecturally diverse VLMs across two rationale-VQA datasets, with sequential-editing experiments, ablations over K, retrieval thresholds, embedding layers, and key merging.

The topology-aware analysis of vision/language modality bias across VLM layers (Figures 6-7, Appendix A) is an interesting empirical contribution in its own right, with scale-invariance of the modularity metric proven.
The paper is generally well written and well organized, with the method clearly delineated from the evaluation protocol.
weaknesses: Potential circularity in the headline evaluation: the R-Gen and CoE-Gen evaluation sets are generated from subsets of the very reasoning sentences stored as codebook values, and their images are synthesized from those same facts. ReasonEdit can therefore retrieve the exact stored sentences used to construct the test questions, giving it a near-oracle advantage on precisely the metrics used to justify the paper's central claim ('human reasoning improves edit generalization'). The GRACE-COT baseline partially controls for this, but the comparison does not isolate whether the gains come from reasoning content or from constructing the test set from the same stored values.

Suspicious baseline implementation: in Table 1, GRACE-COT is essentially identical to GRACE across nearly every metric (e.g., 0.98/0.69/0.92/0.54/0.76/0.99 vs. 0.98/0.69/0.92/0.54/0.76/0.99 on LLaVA-1.5), despite reportedly populating GRACE's codebook with all reasoning facts. This strongly suggests the COT extension of GRACE was not functioning, undermining the fairness of the central comparison. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported anywhere.

The methodological contribution is thinner than the framing suggests: the 'topology-balanced dual embedding' ultimately reduces to concatenating a vision-layer embedding with a pretrained sentence-transformer embedding, and the extensive modularity machinery mainly serves to select the vision layer and a scalar weight w. Heavy formalism (five network-science metrics, Monte Carlo sample networks) is disproportionate to this simple design choice.

Reliability of 1.00 and locality of 1.00 for ReasonEdit are trivially expected for a retrieval-based editor that prepends stored answers and only abstains from retrieval via a percentile threshold; these columns inflate the impression of dominance without adding evidence.

The augmentation procedure underlying bimodal modularity and key merging is questionable: mosaic padding with random Lorem Picsum images and noise is claimed to 'approximate an image that preserves 90% of the semantic meaning,' which is asserted rather than validated, yet the derived metric drives both layer selection and the weight w.

The 'human reasoning' in the interactive editing setup is actually dataset rationales; no user study or realistic feedback-loop evaluation is performed, so claims about real-time usability with human feedback are not directly supported. Only two multiple-choice VQA datasets are used, which limits the claimed reasoning-heavy scope.

Scalability concerns are under-addressed: the no-retrieval threshold requires the p-th percentile of all pairwise key distances (implying O(|C|^2) distances), and KNN over an ever-growing codebook is only partially mitigated by ~20% memory reduction from key merging.

No explicit limitations section; the impact statement is boilerplate. Some claims of being 'the first' are repeated aggressively while the closest prior work (IKE-style retrieval with rationales) differs incrementally.

strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely new problem setting—reasoning-enhanced VLM editing where users provide factual reasoning chains during editing—along with two new evaluation axes (Rationale Generality and Chain-of-Error Generality) that go beyond standard label-flipping metrics in model editing.

The proposed topology-aware embedding analysis (sample modularity, unimodal bias metrics) is a principled and somewhat novel way to select VLM layers and embedding methods for retrieval-based editors; the scale-invariance properties are formally proven, and the layer-wise analysis across four VLM architectures (Figs. 6–7, 13) yields interesting insights about vision/language modality biases across network depth.

Experiments are extensive: four VLMs, two rationale-VQA datasets, five strong baselines plus reasoning-enabled (COT) variants of each baseline, sequential editing over 5,000+ edits, and thorough ablations (embedding method, K, retrieval threshold, key merging), with implementation details and baseline configurations documented in appendices.

The retrieval-based design avoids weight updates, and the paper transparently shows baseline weight-updating editors degrade in sequential editing, supporting the practical motivation. Code and data are promised to be released, and the appendices are detailed enough to support reproduction in principle.
weaknesses: The evaluation design raises circularity concerns that may inflate the headline results. The R-Gen and CoE-Gen evaluation images are synthesized (Stable Diffusion 3 / FLUX) from captions that explicitly append the human reasoning sentences, and R-Gen questions are GPT-4o-generated from the very same fact subsets. Since ReasonEdit's codebook values are exactly these fact sentences, the evaluation may partially test retrieval of the generation prompts rather than genuine generalization. Additionally, for T-Gen/I-Gen/CoE-Gen the question text is unchanged from the edit, so the SBERT component of the dual embedding largely guarantees retrieval regardless of image content—undermining whether image generality is truly being measured.

A critical missing ablation is a text-embedding-only (pure SBERT) key. The ablation compares vision-layer vs. language-layer vs. dual embeddings, but given that the question text is identical between edits and generalization queries in most metrics, a text-only retriever might perform comparably. Without this, the claimed importance of the topology-balanced dual embedding for image generality is not fully supported.

Locality is essentially trivial for ReasonEdit: because the method never modifies weights, locality = 1.00 follows almost by construction (modulo the retrieval threshold), while weight-updating baselines structurally cannot achieve this. Presenting locality as a comparison metric favors retrieval-based editors in a way that should be more clearly acknowledged.

The relationship between GRACE and GRACE-COT in Table 1(a) is confusing—the rows are nearly identical, and the appendix says GRACE's codebook is populated with reasoning entries even in the non-COT case, making the two variants hard to distinguish and raising questions about how the COT augmentation was actually applied.

No statistical significance or multiple-run variance is reported; results appear to be single deterministic runs. Given near-ceiling scores (0.92–1.00) on partially synthetic evaluation sets, error bars and human verification of a sample of generated evaluation data would substantially strengthen the claims.

The 'network science' framing somewhat oversells a method that, in the end, concatenates a vision-layer embedding with an off-the-shelf sentence-transformer embedding and tunes one scalar weight w. The modularity machinery is interesting as analysis, but the final method is a straightforward retrieval/RAG-over-user-feedback design whose novelty over IKE/GRACE-style codebooks is mainly the reasoning entries and evidence patchification.

The modularity and bias estimation relies on synthetic augmentations (mosaic padding with random Lorem Picsum images, ±10° rotation, LLM paraphrases) that are crude proxies for 'semantically equivalent' samples, and the choice of random web images as negatives for language bias is weak; sensitivity to these design choices is not analyzed.

Evaluation is limited to two COCO/ImageNet-grounded multiple-choice VQA datasets; claims of 'reasoning-heavy' editing would be more convincing with at least one harder or open-ended reasoning benchmark, and the dermatology-style motivating example (Fig. 1) is never actually evaluated.

strengths: Novel and practically motivated problem setup: reasoning-enhanced VLM editing where users supply human rationales, with two new evaluation dimensions (rationale generality, chain-of-error generality) that go beyond standard label-flip editing metrics.

The topology-aware embedding analysis (sample modularity, vision/language bias) is an interesting, principled contribution in its own right, with useful empirical insights about modality bias across VLM layers (Fig. 6, Appendix A) and evidence the selection is data-agnostic (Table 4).

Comprehensive experiments: four VLMs, two rationale-VQA datasets, five baselines each augmented with COT variants, static plus sequential editing (5,000 edits), robustness to noisy reasoning, and extensive ablations (K, retrieval threshold, merging, layer-selection criterion).
Fair comparison effort: all baselines receive the same human reasoning inputs (editor-COT variants), and implementation details and hyperparameter configurations are documented in the appendix.
Honest impact statement discussing codebook scalability and the assumption of accurate, structured human reasoning, with an initial noise-robustness study.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the core mechanism is retrieval-augmented prompting (IKE/GRACE-style codebook) with engineered answer/reasoning entries; the main technical additions are dual embedding (concatenating a vision-layer embedding with a sentence-transformer) and heuristic key merging, with hand-set thresholds (90% overlap, 10% of radii) that lack justification or sensitivity analysis.

The headline new metrics (R-Gen, CoE-Gen) are evaluated on datasets synthesized with GPT-4o questions and text-to-image generated images built from the very reasoning facts stored in the codebook. This creates a potential circularity/leakage concern: a retrieval editor storing those exact sentences naturally retrieves them, which may inflate ReasonEdit's advantage over baselines whose retrieved facts are not evaluated on questions derived from those same facts. The quality of these synthetic evaluation sets is not validated by human assessment.

Despite the 'human reasoning' framing, no human user study is conducted; the reasoning comes from dataset annotations, so claims about real-world usability with human feedback (e.g., patch-based visual evidence) remain untested.

Near-perfect reliability (~1.0) and locality (~1.0) for ReasonEdit are largely expected properties of any retrieval-based method storing the edits, so the decisive evidence rests on the generalization metrics whose construction has the concerns above; weight-updating baselines may be disadvantaged by the long free-form output format.

Several important design choices are empirical rather than derived: harmonic-mean criterion for w, percentile p=50 threshold, K=5, and multiple-choice softmax answer extraction; while ablated, the ablations are post hoc rather than principled.
Scalability of exact KNN over a continuously growing codebook (and Monte Carlo modularity estimation at edit time) is acknowledged but not quantified at deployment scale.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant gap: VLM editing for reasoning-heavy VQA where users can supply rationale-style feedback, and the proposed two new evaluation axes (rationale generality, chain-of-error generality) are a useful conceptual framing for the community.

Experiments are extensive: four VLMs across two rationale-VQA datasets, sequential editing over 5,000+ edits, noise robustness, and a fairly complete ablation suite (answer vs. reasoning entries, embedding layer choice, K, rejection threshold, key merging).

The topology-aware embedding analysis (modularity over embedding similarity networks, vision/language bias diagnostics, the w trade-off in Fig. 6/7) is a genuinely interesting empirical contribution on its own, with a data-agnostic hyperparameter selection strategy supported by Table 4.

The paper is generally well written, with honest limitations in the Impact Statement, and reproducibility materials (code, data, detailed appendix including patchification and merging algorithms) appear adequate.
weaknesses: Potential circularity in the headline evaluations. R-Gen questions are generated by GPT-4o from subsets of the very reasoning statements r+ stored as codebook values, and CoE-Gen images are synthesized so the error-inducing facts are visually present while codebook keys are (patch, statement) pairs. Retrieving the stored facts therefore nearly guarantees correct answers on these metrics, so the large R-Gen/CoE-Gen gaps over IKE-COT may partly reflect evaluation construction rather than learned generalization. The paper does not control for this (e.g., retrieving irrelevant reasoning, or human-written unseen rationales).

The core mechanism is conceptually close to existing retrieval-based editors: ReasonEdit is essentially a GRACE/IKE-style codebook that prepends retrieved sentences to the prompt, with added patch-level keys and a dual embedding. The 'first reasoning-enhanced editor' framing overstates novelty; the COT baselines already receive the same reasoning inputs, and the marginal deltas on Acc/T-Gen/I-Gen over IKE-COT are modest in Table 1.

Evaluation protocol deviations weaken comparability with prior editing work: answers are selected via softmax over four multiple-choice options rather than generation, locality is defined only over originally-correct samples, and unedited accuracy is 0 by construction (edit sets are real errors). These choices systematically favor retrieval-based editors and make the strong Loc/Acc claims less informative.

Heavy reliance on synthetic evaluation data: text generality uses GPT-4o rephrasings, image generality and R-Gen/CoE-Gen use SD3/FLUX-generated images validated by the same family of VLM used for editing. Diffusion artifacts and VQA-verifier bias could inflate generality metrics; no human evaluation or real-image hold-out is provided.

Practical assumptions are strong: the method presumes users supply clean, structured, step-by-step factual reasoning plus (ideally) cropped visual evidence per statement, which is costly in realistic deployment; the noise study injects irrelevant sentences but does not test incorrect/wrongly-grounded reasoning, which is the more damaging failure mode.

Scalability and hyperparameter concerns are underexplored: exhaustive ℓ2 search over a growing codebook, sensitivity of results to K and p differing per VLM, and merging thresholds (90%/10%) chosen without clear justification all limit the practical reach of the method, as the authors themselves acknowledge.

Only two multiple-choice VQA datasets (FVQA, A-OKVQA), both COCO/ImageNet-derived; generalization to free-form VQA or genuinely reasoning-heavy domains (e.g., the motivating dermatology example) is asserted via Figure 1 but never evaluated.

strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely new problem setup — reasoning-enhanced VLM editing where users supply human reasoning during editing — which is a meaningful extension beyond existing VLM editing work that mostly handles label/object renaming.

The proposed new evaluation metrics (Rationale Generality and Chain-of-Error Generality) formalize an interesting and previously unmeasured form of edit generalization, and the paper explains their construction in substantial detail (Appendix B).

The topology-aware embedding analysis is a novel and somewhat principled contribution: casting multimodal embeddings as weighted similarity graphs and using Newman's modularity plus vision/language bias metrics to select layers, pooling methods, and the dual-embedding weight w is an interesting cross-disciplinary idea, with useful scale-invariance proofs (Appendix A.4) and a data-agnostic hyperparameter selection result (Table 4).

The empirical evaluation is extensive: four VLMs across two rationale-VQA datasets, five strong baselines plus reasoning-enabled (COT) variants of each, static and sequential editing over 5,000 edits, efficiency measurements, noise-robustness experiments, and thorough ablations (embedding method, K, retrieval threshold, key merging, layer selection criterion).

The ablation in Sec. 4.6 and Table 3 convincingly isolates that reasoning entries (not just answer entries) drive the reasoning-level generalization, and that COT-variants of prior editors do not close the gap — this supports the central claim rather than merely showing aggregate wins.
Honest and specific limitations discussion (codebook search cost, assumption of accurate structured reasoning), and code/data availability supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The new generality evaluation datasets (R-Gen, CoE-Gen, and image-generality sets) are largely synthetic: questions are generated by GPT-4o from reasoning subsets, and images by Stable Diffusion 3/FLUX, with quality verified using a VLM (Qwen3-VL-8B). This introduces potential circularity and distribution mismatch with real user edits; the reported near-perfect R-Gen/CoE-Gen for ReasonEdit (0.84–0.98 vs. ceiling 0.61–0.92) rests on the fidelity of this synthetic pipeline, which is validated only informally.

Reliability is measured via softmax over multiple-choice options rather than free-form generation, following prior benchmark practice. This may inflate Acc (many editors reach ~1.0) and under-detect failures in realistic generation settings; the motivation given (label-flipping brittleness) is reasonable but the trade-off deserves more scrutiny.

The method is architecturally close to retrieval-augmented prompting (IKE-style codebook + context prepending), with the main novelty in patch-based reasoning entries, key merging, and the embedding selection criterion. The modularity-based selection is principled but ultimately a heuristic ranking (harmonic mean of two modularities), and the vision/language 'bias' definitions and the mosaic-padding augmentation underlying bimodal modularity are somewhat ad hoc; the paper would benefit from more justification that the chosen topology truly predicts retrieval quality beyond the observed correlations.

Automatic visual evidence patchification is evaluated only via CLIP similarity being comparable to raw images (Table 5), which is a weak validation; errors in patch selection would propagate into the codebook.

Codebook retrieval is exhaustive ℓ2 search over all keys; scalability beyond thousands of edits is acknowledged as a limitation but not empirically probed, and sequential editing is evaluated on only one dataset.

MSCKE could not be compared (unreleased code) and LiveEdit was excluded due to setup mismatch, so the baseline comparison to the newest VLM-specific editors is incomplete, though the COT-extended baselines mitigate this concern.
